questions.question: How many points does a team get for winning a match?
questions.explanation: Three for a win, one for a draw, nothing for a loss. That is the whole table.

questions.question: How many clubs are in the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Twenty clubs, each playing the others twice. 38 games a season.

questions.question: How many clubs are relegated at the end of a Premier League season?
questions.explanation: The bottom three go down to the Championship and three come up.

questions.question: How long is a match, before any added time?
questions.explanation: Two halves of 45. Added time on top is for stoppages.

questions.question: How many players does each team have on the pitch at kick-off?
questions.explanation: Eleven a side, one of them the goalkeeper.

questions.question: Which colour card means a player is sent off?
questions.explanation: Red is off. Yellow is a warning, and two yellows make a red.

questions.question: Who is the only player allowed to handle the ball inside their own penalty area?
questions.explanation: Only the keeper, and only inside the box. Outside it, same rules as everyone.

questions.question: How far from goal is a penalty kick taken?
questions.explanation: Twelve yards, straight in front of goal, with only the keeper to beat.

questions.question: What does VAR stand for?
questions.explanation: Video Assistant Referee. A team in a room checking the big decisions on replay.

questions.question: How many substitutions can a Premier League team make in a match?
questions.explanation: Five, in three stopped moments, plus half-time. It was three until 2022.

questions.question: What happens when a league match ends level?
questions.explanation: A draw. One point each. Extra time and penalties are for cups.

questions.question: Two yellow cards in one match equals what?
questions.explanation: Two yellows make a red, and the player is off.

questions.question: What is a clean sheet?
questions.explanation: Letting in nothing. The goalkeeper's favourite statistic.

questions.question: A hat-trick is how many goals by one player in one match?
questions.explanation: Three. Two is a brace. The player traditionally keeps the match ball.

questions.question: Which division sits directly below the Premier League?
questions.explanation: The Championship. Confusingly named, since winning it is not really a championship.

questions.question: How many clubs are promoted from the Championship each season?
questions.explanation: Three: the top two automatically, and one more through the play-offs.

questions.question: When two teams finish level on points, what usually separates them?
questions.explanation: Goal difference first: goals scored minus goals conceded.

questions.question: When are the two transfer windows?
questions.explanation: The summer, and the whole of January. Outside those, clubs cannot buy.

questions.question: How long is each half of extra time in a cup match?
questions.explanation: Two halves of fifteen. If it is still level after that, penalties.

questions.question: In a penalty shootout, how many kicks does each side take before it goes to sudden death?
questions.explanation: Five each. Then one at a time until somebody misses.

questions.question: Who takes a corner kick?
questions.explanation: The attackers, after the defending side put the ball out behind their own goal.

questions.question: Which is the oldest cup competition in the world?
questions.explanation: The FA Cup, first played in 1871. Every club in England can enter.

questions.question: What is a match between two local rivals called?
questions.explanation: A derby, pronounced darby. Manchester, Merseyside, North London — all derbies.

questions.question: Which body runs the Champions League?
questions.explanation: UEFA, European football's governing body. FIFA runs the World Cup.

questions.question: Over two legs, what decides which team goes through?
questions.explanation: Add the two scores together. That total is the aggregate.

questions.question: What is nil in football?
questions.explanation: Zero. A goalless draw is nil-nil, and it always will be.

questions.question: What is added time?
options: Time added for a red card
questions.explanation: Minutes tacked on at the end of each half to make up for stoppages.

questions.question: How many yards is the penalty area from the goal line?
questions.explanation: Eighteen yards deep, which is why it is also called the eighteen-yard box.

questions.question: Who has scored the most Premier League goals of all time?
questions.explanation: Alan Shearer, 260. Nobody has got close since.

questions.question: Who has made the most Premier League appearances?
questions.explanation: Gareth Barry, 653 games for Villa, City, Everton and West Brom.

questions.question: Thierry Henry is a legend at which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal. There is a statue of him outside the Emirates.

questions.question: Who managed Manchester United for 26 years until 2013?
questions.explanation: Sir Alex Ferguson. Thirteen league titles. The stand at Old Trafford is named after him.

questions.question: Who scored the injury-time goal that won Manchester City the title in 2012?
questions.explanation: Agüero, 94th minute against QPR. The commentator's 'Agüerooo' is still quoted.

questions.question: Steven Gerrard spent almost his whole career at which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, from 1998 to 2015. Captain, and a Champions League winner in 2005.

questions.question: Which Frenchman managed Arsenal from 1996 to 2018?
questions.explanation: Arsène Wenger. Three league titles and the unbeaten 2003-04 season.

questions.question: Frank Lampard became the all-time record goalscorer of which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, 211 goals. A midfielder, which makes it odder.

questions.question: Who is Tottenham Hotspur's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Harry Kane passed Jimmy Greaves in 2023 before leaving for Bayern Munich.

questions.question: Peter Schmeichel kept goal for which Premier League club in the 1990s?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, five titles. His son Kasper won the league with Leicester in 2016.

questions.question: Eric Cantona was banned for kicking a fan in 1995 while playing for which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, at Selhurst Park. He had joined from Leeds in 1992.

questions.question: Which Welsh winger won thirteen Premier League titles with Manchester United?
questions.explanation: Ryan Giggs, one club for his whole career. Nobody else has thirteen.

questions.question: Dennis Bergkamp, famous for a 1998 World Cup goal, played his club football in England for whom?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, 1995 to 2006. He would not fly, so he missed away games in Europe.

questions.question: Gianfranco Zola, a Chelsea favourite in the late 1990s, came from which country?
questions.explanation: Italy. Small, brilliant, and voted Chelsea's greatest ever player by fans in 2003.

questions.question: Who captained both Manchester United and Ireland and is known as Keano?
questions.explanation: Roy Keane. Fierce midfielder, now a fiercer pundit.

questions.question: Who is Manchester City's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Sergio Agüero, 260 goals in all competitions between 2011 and 2021.

questions.question: Which Liverpool forward is nicknamed the Egyptian King?
questions.explanation: Mohamed Salah, who joined from Roma in 2017 and broke the 38-game scoring record.

questions.question: Didier Drogba scored the winning penalty in the 2012 Champions League final for which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, against Bayern Munich in Munich. He had also scored the late equaliser.

questions.question: Wayne Rooney's famous overhead kick in a 2011 Manchester derby was for which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, at Old Trafford. Voted the best goal in twenty years of the Premier League.

questions.question: Who captained Manchester City to their first Premier League title in 2012?
questions.explanation: Vincent Kompany, the Belgian centre-back who later became a manager.

questions.question: Who scored the fastest Premier League hat-trick, in under three minutes for Southampton in 2015?
questions.explanation: Sadio Mané, two minutes and 56 seconds against Aston Villa.

questions.question: Jamie Vardy set a record in 2015 by scoring in how many consecutive Premier League matches?
questions.explanation: Eleven in a row for Leicester, beating Ruud van Nistelrooy's ten.

questions.question: Who managed Leicester City to the 2016 Premier League title?
questions.explanation: Claudio Ranieri. Leicester started the season as 5000-1 outsiders.

questions.question: Robin van Persie left Arsenal in 2012 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, where he won the title and the Golden Boot in his first season.

questions.question: Which Belgian midfielder was Manchester City's playmaker for a decade from 2015?
questions.explanation: Kevin De Bruyne. Passes nobody else saw, and six league titles.

questions.question: David Beckham scored from the halfway line in 1996 against Wimbledon playing for whom?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, on the opening day of the season. It made him famous overnight.

questions.question: Which Arsenal team went a whole Premier League season unbeaten?
questions.explanation: 2003-04. 26 wins, 12 draws, no defeats. They are called the Invincibles.

questions.question: Who was the first player to score 100 Premier League goals?
questions.explanation: Alan Shearer, in 1995 for Blackburn Rovers, who won the title that year.

questions.question: The North London derby is between Arsenal and which club?
questions.explanation: Spurs. Four miles apart and about as friendly as it sounds.

questions.question: Which two clubs play the Merseyside derby?
questions.explanation: Liverpool and Everton, whose grounds were a short walk apart across Stanley Park.

questions.question: The Manchester derby is City against whom?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. City fans spent decades in United's shadow, which is why it matters so much now.

questions.question: Which two clubs contest the M23 derby?
questions.explanation: Brighton and Crystal Palace, named after the motorway between them. Genuinely bitter.

questions.question: The Tyne-Wear derby is Newcastle against which club?
questions.explanation: Sunderland. Two rivers, twelve miles, over a century of not getting on.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Gunners?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, founded by workers at a royal armaments factory in Woolwich.

questions.question: Which club is known as the Toffees?
questions.explanation: Everton. Named after a toffee shop near the ground; a Toffee Lady still throws sweets to the crowd.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Magpies?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, for the black and white stripes.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Cherries?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth. Cherry-red shirts, and cherry orchards near the old ground.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Bees?
questions.explanation: Brentford. The badge is a bee and the fans chant 'buzz'.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Seagulls?
questions.explanation: Brighton. It started as a chant to wind up Palace fans, who sing 'Eagles'.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Villans?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa. Villa, Villans. Not villains, though rivals disagree.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Cottagers?
questions.explanation: Fulham, whose ground is Craven Cottage, with an actual cottage in the corner.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Black Cats?
questions.explanation: Sunderland. A black cat was a lucky mascot at a cup final over a century ago.

questions.question: Which club plays in claret and blue and has Birmingham City as its city rival?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa. The Second City derby, when Birmingham are in the same division.

questions.question: Which two clubs contest the East Anglian derby?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town and Norwich City. Forty miles apart and it is the biggest game of either club's year.

questions.question: Leeds United's rivalry with Manchester United is known as which war?
questions.explanation: The Roses rivalry, Yorkshire's white rose against Lancashire's red. Older than football.

questions.question: Who are Chelsea's closest West London neighbours in the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Fulham. Stamford Bridge and Craven Cottage are under two miles apart.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Sky Blues?
questions.explanation: Coventry City. Sky blue shirts since the 1960s, and the fans' nickname since then too.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Tractor Boys?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town. Suffolk farming country. Started as an insult from rival fans and got adopted.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Tigers?
questions.explanation: Hull City, for the amber and black stripes.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Eagles?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace. An actual eagle used to be flown around Selhurst Park before games.

questions.question: Which club's fans sing 'You'll Never Walk Alone' before every home game?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, since the 1960s. The words are over the gates at Anfield.

questions.question: Nottingham Forest's fiercest rivalry is with which club?
questions.explanation: Derby County. Fifteen miles apart, and Brian Clough managed both.

questions.question: Spurs is short for which club?
questions.explanation: Tottenham Hotspur, named after Harry Hotspur, a medieval knight from Shakespeare.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Red Devils?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. Matt Busby liked the name in the 1960s and it stuck.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Whites?
questions.explanation: Leeds United, who switched to all-white in the 1960s to copy Real Madrid.

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Tricky Trees?
questions.explanation: Nottingham Forest. The badge is a tree; the trickiness is aspirational.

questions.question: Which club plays at the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, since 2006. Before that, Highbury, a few hundred yards away.

questions.question: Anfield is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. Originally Everton's ground, until a rent row in 1892.

questions.question: Old Trafford is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, since 1910. Nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams.

questions.question: Stamford Bridge is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea. The club was founded in 1905 to fill a stadium that already existed.

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a cockerel standing on a football?
questions.explanation: Spurs. There has been a cockerel on the badge and the stadium roof since 1909.

questions.question: Which club's badge features the liver bird?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. The liver bird is the city's symbol, a cormorant with seaweed in its beak.

questions.question: Villa Park is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa, since 1897. It has hosted more FA Cup semi-finals than any other ground.

questions.question: Goodison Park was for over a century the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Everton, from 1892 until they moved to a new stadium on the docks in 2025.

questions.question: St James' Park is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Newcastle. Right in the city centre; the stadium looks over the shops.

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a red devil holding a trident?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. The devil has been on the badge since 1970.

questions.question: Which club has a cannon on its badge?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, for the Royal Arsenal armaments works where the club began.

questions.question: Which club's badge is a bee?
questions.explanation: Brentford. Red and white stripes, and a bee.

questions.question: Which club's badge shows an eagle perched on a football?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace, above a drawing of the original glass palace the club is named after.

questions.question: Craven Cottage is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Fulham, on the Thames. Oldest professional football ground in London.

questions.question: The City Ground is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Nottingham Forest, on the banks of the River Trent.

questions.question: Which club plays at the Stadium of Light?
questions.explanation: Sunderland, since 1997. Benfica's ground in Lisbon has the same name.

questions.question: Elland Road is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Leeds United, since 1919. Famous for its noise.

questions.question: The Vitality Stadium is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth. Its old name is Dean Court; it holds barely 11,000.

questions.question: Which club plays at the ground known as the Amex?
questions.explanation: Brighton, at Falmer, on the edge of the South Downs.

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a ship above three diagonal stripes for the city's rivers?
questions.explanation: Manchester City. The ship is for trade on the Manchester Ship Canal, with a red rose for Lancashire.

questions.question: Portman Road is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town, since 1884.

questions.question: Selhurst Park is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace, in South London. Wimbledon and Charlton have both shared it.

questions.question: The Gtech Community Stadium is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Brentford, since 2020, replacing Griffin Park, the ground with a pub on every corner.

questions.question: Which club plays at the MKM Stadium?
questions.explanation: Hull City, since 2002. It was the KC Stadium before a sponsor changed its name.

questions.question: Which club's badge features a tree?
questions.explanation: Nottingham Forest. A tree with wavy lines for the River Trent, designed by a fan in 1973.

questions.question: Which club's badge has a white rose above the shield?
questions.explanation: Leeds United. The white rose of Yorkshire.

questions.question: Which ground is nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams?
questions.explanation: Old Trafford. Bobby Charlton coined it.

questions.question: Where do England play their home matches?
questions.explanation: Wembley, in north-west London. The arch is visible from across the city.

questions.question: In which year was Arsenal founded?
questions.explanation: 1886, by workers at the Royal Arsenal munitions factory in Woolwich. Hence the cannon.

questions.question: Where did Arsenal play before the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: Highbury, from 1913 to 2006. The old stands are flats now, with the pitch as a garden.

questions.question: What is Arsenal's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Gunners, for the armaments works. The fans are Gooners.

questions.question: In which season did Arsenal go the whole league campaign unbeaten?
questions.explanation: 2003-04: 26 wins, 12 draws, no defeats. The team is known as the Invincibles.

questions.question: Who managed the Invincibles?
questions.explanation: Arsène Wenger, in charge from 1996 to 2018. The longest-serving manager in the club's history.

questions.question: In which part of London did Arsenal begin life?
questions.explanation: Woolwich, in south-east London. They moved north to Highbury in 1913, which Spurs have never forgiven.

questions.question: Who is Arsenal's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Thierry Henry, 228 goals across two spells. He has a statue outside the ground.

questions.question: What colour are Arsenal's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red body, white sleeves, since 1933. Herbert Chapman's idea.

questions.question: Which club has won the FA Cup more times than any other?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, fourteen times, the last of them in 2020.

questions.question: Who managed Arsenal to league titles in 1989 and 1991?
questions.explanation: George Graham, a former Arsenal player. Famous for a mean defence: 'one-nil to the Arsenal'.

questions.question: Who scored the last-minute goal at Anfield that won Arsenal the 1989 title?
questions.explanation: Michael Thomas, in the final minute of the final game. Arsenal needed to win by two and did.

questions.question: Who captained the Invincibles?
questions.explanation: Patrick Vieira, the French midfielder who later became a manager.

questions.question: Which goalkeeper played for Arsenal for most of the 1990s?
questions.explanation: David Seaman, ponytail and all. England's keeper for over a decade.

questions.question: Who are Arsenal's biggest rivals?
questions.explanation: Tottenham. The North London derby. Not a friendly fixture.

questions.question: In which year did Arsenal move to the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: 2006. The move was expensive, and the club went nine years without a trophy afterwards.

questions.question: Which 1930s manager, who brought in the white sleeves, has a statue outside the Emirates?
questions.explanation: Herbert Chapman. He also got the local Tube station renamed Arsenal — the only one named after a club.

questions.question: Tony Adams captained Arsenal to league titles in how many different decades?
questions.explanation: Three: 1989 and 1991, 1998, and 2002. Nobody else in England has done that.

questions.question: In which year did Arsenal reach their only Champions League final?
questions.explanation: 2006, in Paris. They lost 2-1 to Barcelona after playing most of the game with ten men.

questions.question: What is the name of Arsenal's dinosaur mascot?
questions.explanation: Gunnersaurus Rex, since 1993. Briefly made redundant in 2020, then reinstated after an outcry.

questions.question: Dennis Bergkamp's famous turn-and-finish goal in 2002 was against which club?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, at St James' Park. He flicked it one side of the defender and ran round the other.

questions.question: What is Aston Villa's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Villa Park, since 1897. The famous stand behind the goal is the Holte End.

questions.question: What colours do Aston Villa play in?
questions.explanation: Claret and blue. West Ham and Burnley borrowed the combination from Villa.

questions.question: In which year was Aston Villa founded?
questions.explanation: 1874, by members of a Wesleyan chapel cricket team who wanted something to do in winter.

questions.question: In which year did Aston Villa win the European Cup?
questions.explanation: 1982, beating Bayern Munich 1-0 in Rotterdam. Only a handful of English clubs have won it.

questions.question: Who scored the winning goal in the 1982 European Cup final?
questions.explanation: Peter Withe, off his shin, from a Tony Morley cross. 'Withe' is painted on the goalpost at Villa Park.

questions.question: Who are Aston Villa's city rivals?
questions.explanation: Birmingham City. The Second City derby, whenever both are in the same division.

questions.question: Aston Villa were founder members of which competition in 1888?
questions.explanation: The Football League, the world's first. A Villa director, William McGregor, came up with the idea.

questions.question: How many English league titles has Aston Villa won?
questions.explanation: Seven, the last in 1981. Only a few clubs have more.

questions.question: Who managed Aston Villa to the league title in 1981?
questions.explanation: Ron Saunders, who used just fourteen players all season. He left months before the European Cup win.

questions.question: Which academy midfielder captained Villa before leaving in 2009 for Manchester City?
questions.explanation: Gareth Barry, who went on to make more Premier League appearances than anyone.

questions.question: Jack Grealish left Aston Villa in 2021 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, for a British record £100 million. He had been Villa captain.

questions.question: After relegation in 2016, in which year did Villa return to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2019, beating Derby in the play-off final at Wembley.

questions.question: What is Aston Villa's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Villans. Spelt with an a. Rival fans prefer the other spelling.

questions.question: Which striker left Villa for Manchester United in 1998 and won the treble the next year?
questions.explanation: Dwight Yorke, from Trinidad and Tobago. Villa fans were not pleased.

questions.question: Which Villa goalkeeper won the World Cup with Argentina in 2022?
questions.explanation: Emiliano Martínez, who also won the Golden Glove at the tournament.

questions.question: The Holte End is a famous stand at which ground?
questions.explanation: Villa Park. One of the biggest single stands in England.

questions.question: Who was Villa's manager for the 1982 European Cup final, having taken over mid-season?
questions.explanation: Tony Barton, promoted from assistant when Saunders quit in February. He won the biggest prize three months later.

questions.question: Villa beat Manchester United in the 1994 League Cup final under which manager?
questions.explanation: Ron Atkinson, who had managed United himself. It stopped United winning a domestic treble.

questions.question: Aston Villa are from which city?
questions.explanation: Birmingham. Aston is a district of the city, north of the centre.

questions.question: Which animal is on the Aston Villa badge?
questions.explanation: A lion, taken from the Scottish royal standard. An early chairman was Scottish.

questions.question: What is Bournemouth's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Vitality Stadium, also known by its old name, Dean Court.

questions.question: What is Bournemouth's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Cherries. Cherry-red shirts, and cherry orchards near the original ground.

questions.question: In which year did Bournemouth first reach the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2015, for the first time in the club's history.

questions.question: Which manager took Bournemouth from League Two to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Eddie Howe, a former Bournemouth defender. Two spells, three promotions.

questions.question: What colours are Bournemouth's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and black stripes, modelled on AC Milan's kit in the early 1970s.

questions.question: Bournemouth is in which English county?
questions.explanation: Dorset, on the south coast. Beaches, pines, and a very small football ground.

questions.question: In which year did Bournemouth go into administration and nearly go out of business?
questions.explanation: 2008. They started the next season on minus 17 points and stayed up. Seven years later they were in the Premier League.

questions.question: How many seasons did Bournemouth's first Premier League spell last?
questions.explanation: Five, from 2015 to 2020, when they were relegated on the final day.

questions.question: After relegation in 2020, in which year did Bournemouth return to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2022, finishing second in the Championship.

questions.question: Bournemouth is on which coast of England?
questions.explanation: The south coast, between Southampton and Poole.

questions.question: Which manager led Bournemouth back to the Premier League in 2022?
questions.explanation: Scott Parker, the former England midfielder. He was sacked four games into the following season.

questions.question: What does Bournemouth's badge show?
questions.explanation: A player heading the ball, in profile, on red and black stripes.

questions.question: Who are Bournemouth's south-coast rivals?
questions.explanation: Southampton, thirty miles up the road. The bigger club historically, which Bournemouth enjoy pointing out has changed.

questions.question: Roughly how many people does Bournemouth's ground hold?
questions.explanation: About 11,000. The smallest ground in Premier League history.

questions.question: Bournemouth striker Callum Wilson left in 2020 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, where he kept scoring. He had been Bournemouth's top scorer in the top flight.

questions.question: Andoni Iraola, appointed Bournemouth manager in 2023, is from which country?
questions.explanation: Spain, from the Basque Country. He had managed Rayo Vallecano in Madrid.

questions.question: After leaving Bournemouth in 2020, Eddie Howe went on to manage which club?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, from 2021, taking them into the Champions League.

questions.question: What does AFC stand for in AFC Bournemouth?
questions.explanation: Athletic Football Club. The club put the letters first in 1971 so it would appear at the top of alphabetical lists.

questions.question: What was Bournemouth called before 1971?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic. Boscombe is the suburb where the ground is.

questions.question: In which division did Bournemouth play in 2009, six years before reaching the Premier League?
questions.explanation: League Two, the fourth tier, and fighting relegation from it. One of the fastest rises in English football.

questions.question: What is Brentford's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Bees. The badge is a bee and the fans chant 'buzz'.

questions.question: What is Brentford's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Gtech Community Stadium, by Kew Bridge, since 2020.

questions.question: What was the name of Brentford's old ground, famous for a pub on every corner?
questions.explanation: Griffin Park, their home from 1904 to 2020. Four pubs, one on each corner.

questions.question: In which year were Brentford promoted to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2021, beating Swansea 2-0 in the play-off final at Wembley.

questions.question: What colours are Brentford's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and white stripes, with black shorts.

questions.question: Which Danish manager took Brentford into the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Thomas Frank, in charge from 2018. He stayed seven years.

questions.question: Brentford's owner, known for using statistics and betting models, is who?
questions.explanation: Matthew Benham, a lifelong fan who made his money in sports betting. He owns Danish club Midtjylland too.

questions.question: Brentford is in which part of London?
questions.explanation: West London, near Kew Gardens, sandwiched between Fulham and QPR.

questions.question: When Brentford were promoted in 2021, how long had it been since they were last in the top flight?
questions.explanation: 74 years. Their previous top-flight season was 1946-47.

questions.question: Ivan Toney left Brentford in 2024 to play in which country?
questions.explanation: Saudi Arabia, joining Al-Ahli. He had been Brentford's top scorer for four seasons.

questions.question: Who are Brentford's nearest rivals?
questions.explanation: Fulham and Queens Park Rangers, both a few miles away in west London.

questions.question: What is on the Brentford badge?
questions.explanation: A bee, in a red and white circle.

questions.question: In 2016 Brentford closed their youth academy and replaced it with what?
questions.explanation: A B team for players released elsewhere aged 17 to 20. Several went on to the first team.

questions.question: Brentford's first ever Premier League match in 2021 was a 2-0 home win over which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, on the opening Friday night of the season. A fine way to arrive.

questions.question: What is Brentford's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Buzz Bee. Not a complicated one.

questions.question: Christian Eriksen joined Brentford in 2022 after a cardiac arrest at which tournament?
questions.explanation: Euro 2020, played in 2021, when he collapsed on the pitch for Denmark. He was fitted with a defibrillator.

questions.question: Brentford's stadium sits beside which London landmark?
questions.explanation: Kew Bridge, over the Thames. The stadium is squeezed between railway lines.

questions.question: At which stadium did Brentford win the 2021 play-off final?
questions.explanation: Wembley, in front of a limited crowd during the pandemic.

questions.question: In which year was Brentford founded?
questions.explanation: 1889, by members of a rowing club looking for a winter sport. They chose football over rugby by a vote.

questions.question: Thomas Frank left Brentford in 2025 to manage which club?
questions.explanation: Tottenham. Brentford lost their manager, captain and top scorer in the same summer.

questions.question: What is Brighton's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Seagulls. It began as a chant to answer Crystal Palace fans singing 'Eagles'.

questions.question: What is Brighton's home ground commonly called?
questions.explanation: The Amex, at Falmer, after the sponsor. Officially the American Express Stadium.

questions.question: Who are Brighton's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace, forty miles away. The M23 derby, and it is genuinely heated.

questions.question: In which year were Brighton promoted to the Premier League for the first time?
questions.explanation: 2017, after 34 years out of the top flight.

questions.question: Which manager took Brighton into the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Chris Hughton, who kept them up for two seasons before being sacked.

questions.question: What colours are Brighton's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Blue and white stripes.

questions.question: Brighton's owner, a professional gambler and lifelong fan, is who?
questions.explanation: Tony Bloom, known as the Lizard at the poker table. His data company finds Brighton's bargains.

questions.question: Which Italian manager took Brighton into Europe for the first time?
questions.explanation: Roberto De Zerbi, who took them to sixth in 2023 and the Europa League.

questions.question: Which ground did Brighton lose in 1997, leaving them homeless for two years?
questions.explanation: The Goldstone Ground, sold by the owners. They played home games in Gillingham for two seasons.

questions.question: Brighton reached the FA Cup final in 1983 and lost the replay to which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, 4-0 in the replay after a 2-2 draw. 'And Smith must score' is still quoted.

questions.question: Graham Potter left Brighton in 2022 to manage which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea. It did not go well, and he was sacked within seven months.

questions.question: Brighton sold Moisés Caicedo to Chelsea in 2023 for roughly how much?
questions.explanation: About £115 million, a British record at the time. Brighton had paid Independiente del Valle around £4 million.

questions.question: Brighton is in which county?
questions.explanation: Sussex, on the south coast. The ground is on the edge of the South Downs.

questions.question: Which Brighton midfielder moved to Liverpool in 2023, shortly after winning the World Cup?
questions.explanation: Alexis Mac Allister, a World Cup winner with Argentina in December 2022.

questions.question: In which competition did Brighton play their first ever European campaign in 2023-24?
questions.explanation: The Europa League. They reached the last 16, beating Ajax and Marseille along the way.

questions.question: Where did Brighton play their home games between 1999 and 2011?
questions.explanation: Withdean, a converted athletics track with temporary stands. Fans called it the Theatre of Trees.

questions.question: The Brighton v Crystal Palace rivalry is named after what?
questions.explanation: The M23 motorway that links the two. The actual origin was a 1970s feud between the managers.

questions.question: In which year was Brighton & Hove Albion founded?
questions.explanation: 1901, replacing a club called Brighton United that had gone bust.

questions.question: What is Brighton's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Gully, a seagull, and a second one called Gully's Girl.

questions.question: In which year did Brighton's Amex Stadium open?
questions.explanation: 2011, after a fourteen-year fight for planning permission. The first league game was a 2-1 win over Doncaster.

questions.question: What is Chelsea's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Stamford Bridge, in Fulham. The ground existed before the club, which was founded to fill it.

questions.question: In which year was Chelsea founded?
questions.explanation: 1905, in a pub called the Rising Sun opposite the ground. It is now called the Butcher's Hook.

questions.question: What colour are Chelsea's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Royal blue, since the early 1960s. Before that a lighter Eton blue.

questions.question: Which Russian billionaire owned Chelsea from 2003 to 2022?
questions.explanation: Roman Abramovich. Nineteen trophies in nineteen years, and a lot of sacked managers.

questions.question: In which year did Chelsea first win the Champions League?
questions.explanation: 2012, in Munich, on penalties against Bayern in their own stadium.

questions.question: Who did Chelsea beat in the 2021 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, 1-0 in Porto. Kai Havertz scored the goal.

questions.question: Who is Chelsea's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Frank Lampard, 211 goals. He was a midfielder, which makes it more remarkable.

questions.question: Which manager won Chelsea back-to-back league titles in 2005 and 2006?
questions.explanation: José Mourinho, the self-styled Special One, in his first spell. He came back in 2013 and won another.

questions.question: In which year did Chelsea win their first league title?
questions.explanation: 1955, exactly fifty years before the second one. Chelsea fans waited a long time.

questions.question: Which centre-back captained Chelsea for over a decade and was known as Captain, Leader, Legend?
questions.explanation: John Terry, from 2004 to 2017. Five league titles as captain.

questions.question: Which Ivorian striker scored in four FA Cup finals for Chelsea?
questions.explanation: Didier Drogba, who scored in every final he played in for Chelsea. A man for the big day.

questions.question: The Shed End is a stand at which ground?
questions.explanation: Stamford Bridge. The old terrace behind the south goal, where the loudest fans stood.

questions.question: Which Italian manager led Chelsea to the league and cup double in 2010, scoring 103 league goals?
questions.explanation: Carlo Ancelotti. The 103 goals were a Premier League record at the time.

questions.question: Antonio Conte's 2017 title-winning Chelsea side was famous for switching to which formation?
questions.explanation: 3-4-3, after a bad start. They won thirteen league games in a row once he changed it.

questions.question: Which manager led Chelsea Women to a run of Women's Super League titles before leaving in 2024?
questions.explanation: Emma Hayes, seven league titles in twelve years, then off to coach the United States.

questions.question: What is Chelsea's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Blues. They were the Pensioners until the 1950s, after the Chelsea war veterans who lived nearby.

questions.question: Which Chelsea goalkeeper saved a penalty in the shootout of the 2012 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Petr Čech, wearing his famous protective headguard. He also saved one in extra time.

questions.question: Who are Chelsea's closest neighbours in West London?
questions.explanation: Fulham. Craven Cottage is under two miles away along the river.

questions.question: Which Italian became Chelsea's player-manager in 1998?
questions.explanation: Gianluca Vialli, taking over from Ruud Gullit. He won the League Cup and the Cup Winners' Cup in his first months.

questions.question: Eden Hazard left Chelsea in 2019 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Real Madrid, after seven seasons. He scored twice in his last game, the Europa League final.

questions.question: What is Coventry City's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Sky Blues, for the shirts. The fans have sung the Sky Blue Song since the 1960s.

questions.question: In which year did Coventry City win the FA Cup?
questions.explanation: 1987, the club's only major trophy. The city partied for a week.

questions.question: Who did Coventry beat in the 1987 FA Cup final?
questions.explanation: Tottenham, 3-2 after extra time. Spurs had never lost an FA Cup final before.

questions.question: What colour are Coventry's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Sky blue, since 1962. Before that they had played in almost every colour going.

questions.question: Coventry City were founded in 1883 under what name?
questions.explanation: Singers FC, the works team of a bicycle factory. They became Coventry City in 1898.

questions.question: Which manager introduced the sky blue kit and wrote the Sky Blue Song in the 1960s?
questions.explanation: Jimmy Hill, later the presenter of Match of the Day. He took them from the third tier to the first.

questions.question: What was Coventry's home ground from 1899 to 2005?
questions.explanation: Highfield Road, close to the city centre. It is housing now.

questions.question: Highfield Road became the first ground in England to be what, in 1981?
questions.explanation: All-seater. Fans hated it and the terraces came back within a few years.

questions.question: When Coventry went down in 2001, how many seasons in a row had they spent in the top flight?
questions.explanation: 34, since 1967. Only a handful of clubs had a longer unbroken run at the time.

questions.question: What is the current name of the stadium Coventry moved into in 2005?
questions.explanation: The CBS Arena, after a sponsor. It opened as the Ricoh Arena.

questions.question: In 2013-14 Coventry played their home games in which town because of a rent dispute?
questions.explanation: Northampton, 35 miles away. Attendances collapsed and fans protested outside the empty Ricoh.

questions.question: From 2019 to 2021 Coventry shared a ground with which club?
questions.explanation: Birmingham City, at St Andrew's. They won promotion to the Championship while playing there.

questions.question: Which manager took Coventry from League Two to a Championship play-off final?
questions.explanation: Mark Robins, in charge from 2017 to 2024. He had scored for the club as a player.

questions.question: Coventry lost the 2023 Championship play-off final on penalties to which club?
questions.explanation: Luton Town, after a 1-1 draw at Wembley. Luton went up to the Premier League instead.

questions.question: Coventry's winning goal in the 1987 FA Cup final was an own goal by which Spurs player?
questions.explanation: Gary Mabbutt, whose knee deflected a cross into his own net in extra time. A Coventry fanzine was named after the knee.

questions.question: Coventry is in which region of England?
questions.explanation: The West Midlands, about twenty miles from Birmingham.

questions.question: Which club is Coventry's main Midlands rival?
questions.explanation: Birmingham City, with Leicester and Aston Villa not far behind in the dislike rankings.

questions.question: Which striker shared the Premier League Golden Boot in 1998 with 18 goals for Coventry?
questions.explanation: Dion Dublin, level with Michael Owen and Chris Sutton. He later became a TV presenter.

questions.question: Which former England midfielder was appointed Coventry manager in November 2024?
questions.explanation: Frank Lampard, his first job since a difficult spell back at Chelsea.

questions.question: The Sky Blue Song is sung to the tune of what?
questions.explanation: The Eton Boating Song. Jimmy Hill wrote the words with the club secretary in 1962.

questions.question: In which division were Coventry playing in 2017-18, the season before their climb began?
questions.explanation: League Two, the fourth tier, the lowest the club had ever been. They won the play-offs that May.

questions.question: What is Crystal Palace's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Selhurst Park, in south London, since 1924.

questions.question: What is Crystal Palace's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Eagles, since 1973. Before that they were the Glaziers, after the glass palace.

questions.question: Who are Crystal Palace's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Brighton, forty miles down the M23. Nobody outside the two clubs quite understands it.

questions.question: What colours are Palace's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and blue vertical stripes, modelled on Barcelona in the 1970s.

questions.question: In which year was Crystal Palace founded?
questions.explanation: 1905, by workers at the Crystal Palace exhibition building. They played in the grounds at first.

questions.question: Which former England manager took charge of Palace in 2017, the club he supported as a boy?
questions.explanation: Roy Hodgson, who grew up in Croydon and watched Palace from the terraces.

questions.question: Palace lost FA Cup finals in 1990 and 2016 to the same club. Which?
questions.explanation: Manchester United both times, the first after a replay and the second in extra time.

questions.question: Crystal Palace won their first major trophy in 2025. Which one?
questions.explanation: The FA Cup, beating Manchester City 1-0 at Wembley. 120 years without a trophy, then that.

questions.question: Who scored the winning goal in the 2025 FA Cup final?
questions.explanation: Eberechi Eze, in the first half. Palace's goalkeeper Dean Henderson then saved a penalty.

questions.question: Wilfried Zaha, Palace's most-capped Premier League player, left in 2023 for which club?
questions.explanation: Galatasaray in Turkey, after two spells and over 450 games for Palace.

questions.question: Which striker scored twice off the bench in the 1990 FA Cup final for Palace?
questions.explanation: Ian Wright, playing with a broken leg that had only just healed. United won the replay.

questions.question: What is Crystal Palace named after?
questions.explanation: The Crystal Palace, the huge glass hall from the Great Exhibition of 1851. It burned down in 1936.

questions.question: What is the name of the real eagle that flew around Selhurst Park before matches?
questions.explanation: Kayla, an American bald eagle, from 2010 until her retirement. Fans miss her.

questions.question: Crystal Palace are from which part of London?
questions.explanation: South London, around Croydon and Selhurst.

questions.question: In 1989 Palace lost 9-0 to which club, the Premier League era's precursor to their worst defeat?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, at Anfield. Palace got revenge months later, beating them 4-3 in the FA Cup semi-final.

questions.question: Who scored the extra-time winner in Palace's 4-3 FA Cup semi-final win over Liverpool in 1990?
questions.explanation: Alan Pardew, who later came back to manage the club and took them to the 2016 final.

questions.question: Which former Arsenal captain managed Palace from 2021 to 2023?
questions.explanation: Patrick Vieira. He was sacked after a run of twelve games without a win.

questions.question: The fan group behind the drums and flags at Selhurst Park is called what?
questions.explanation: The Holmesdale Fanatics, named after the stand they fill. The best atmosphere in London, by some accounts.

questions.question: Palace won promotion to the Premier League in 2004 by beating which club in the play-off final?
questions.explanation: West Ham, 1-0 in Cardiff. Neil Shipperley scored the goal.

questions.question: Which Austrian manager won the FA Cup with Palace in 2025?
questions.explanation: Oliver Glasner, who had already won the Europa League with Eintracht Frankfurt.

questions.question: Which ground was Everton's home from 1892 to 2025?
questions.explanation: Goodison Park, the first purpose-built football stadium in England. They moved to the docks in 2025.

questions.question: What is Everton's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Toffees, after a sweet shop near the ground. A Toffee Lady still throws sweets before games.

questions.question: Who are Everton's rivals in the Merseyside derby?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. The friendly derby, they say, though it has had more red cards than any other fixture.

questions.question: In which year was Everton founded?
questions.explanation: 1878, as St Domingo's, a church team. They changed the name a year later.

questions.question: What colour are Everton's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Royal blue, since 1901. Before that they tried black with a red sash.

questions.question: Who is Everton's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Dixie Dean, 383 goals in the 1920s and 30s. There is a statue of him outside Goodison.

questions.question: How many league goals did Dixie Dean score in the 1927-28 season, still a record?
questions.explanation: Sixty, in 39 games. He got the last three in the final match to break the record.

questions.question: In which year did Everton last win the league?
questions.explanation: 1987, under Howard Kendall. They also won it in 1985.

questions.question: Who managed Everton through their 1980s glory years?
questions.explanation: Howard Kendall, two league titles, an FA Cup and a European trophy in three seasons.

questions.question: Which European trophy did Everton win in 1985?
questions.explanation: The Cup Winners' Cup, beating Rapid Vienna 3-1 in Rotterdam. Then English clubs were banned from Europe.

questions.question: In which year did Everton win their last major trophy, the FA Cup?
questions.explanation: 1995, beating Manchester United 1-0 at Wembley. Paul Rideout scored.

questions.question: Wayne Rooney made his first-team debut for which club?
questions.explanation: Everton, aged sixteen. His first goal, against Arsenal, ended a 30-game unbeaten run.

questions.question: Which Scottish manager had two spells at Everton, from 2002 to 2013 and again from 2025?
questions.explanation: David Moyes. He called Everton the People's Club on his first day and it stuck.

questions.question: Which club has spent more seasons in England's top division than any other?
questions.explanation: Everton, relegated only twice in their history, most recently in 1951.

questions.question: Where does the nickname the Toffees come from?
questions.explanation: Mother Noblett's toffee shop near the ground, which sold Everton Mints to fans.

questions.question: Everton's new stadium, opened in 2025, is built where?
questions.explanation: Bramley-Moore Dock, on the Mersey waterfront north of the city centre.

questions.question: Where did Everton play before moving to Goodison Park in 1892?
questions.explanation: Anfield. A row over rent saw Everton leave, and the landlord started a new club there: Liverpool.

questions.question: Tim Cahill, famous for punching the corner flag when he scored, is from which country?
questions.explanation: Australia. He scored 56 Everton goals and boxed a lot of corner flags.

questions.question: In which position did Everton finish in 2005, earning a Champions League qualifying place?
questions.explanation: Fourth, above Liverpool, who then won the Champions League that same season. Everton fans do not enjoy that detail.

questions.question: The Gwladys Street End was the home fans' stand at which ground?
questions.explanation: Goodison Park. The team always tried to attack towards it in the second half.

questions.question: What is Fulham's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Craven Cottage, on the bank of the Thames. There really is a cottage in one corner.

questions.question: What is Fulham's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Cottagers, after the cottage in the corner of the ground.

questions.question: In which year was Fulham founded?
questions.explanation: 1879, as a church team. They are London's oldest professional club.

questions.question: What colours are Fulham's home kit?
questions.explanation: White shirts, black shorts. Simple and old-fashioned, like the ground.

questions.question: Which Egyptian businessman owned Fulham from 1997 to 2013?
questions.explanation: Mohamed Al-Fayed, who also owned Harrods. He took them from the third tier to the Premier League.

questions.question: A statue of which pop star stood outside Craven Cottage from 2011 to 2014?
questions.explanation: Michael Jackson, a friend of Al-Fayed who had watched one game there. Fans were baffled; the next owner removed it.

questions.question: In which year did Fulham reach the Europa League final?
questions.explanation: 2010, losing 2-1 to Atlético Madrid in Hamburg after extra time. A remarkable run for a small club.

questions.question: Who managed Fulham to the 2010 Europa League final?
questions.explanation: Roy Hodgson, who was named manager of the year and then took the Liverpool job.

questions.question: Which American businessman bought Fulham in 2013?
questions.explanation: Shahid Khan, who also owns the Jacksonville Jaguars NFL team.

questions.question: Craven Cottage sits beside which river?
questions.explanation: The Thames. Fans can watch the rowers go past before the game.

questions.question: Fulham won promotion as champions of the second tier in 2001 under which French manager?
questions.explanation: Jean Tigana, with 101 points. It was Fulham's first time in the top flight since 1968.

questions.question: Which Portuguese manager won the Championship with Fulham in 2022?
questions.explanation: Marco Silva, with Mitrović scoring goals for fun. Fulham finally stopped bouncing between divisions.

questions.question: Who are Fulham's main London rivals?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, less than two miles away. Brentford and QPR are the other local grudges.

questions.question: Johnny Haynes, the first footballer to be paid £100 a week, spent his whole career at which club?
questions.explanation: Fulham, 1952 to 1970. A stand at Craven Cottage is named after him and he has a statue outside.

questions.question: Which American scored the goal that knocked Juventus out of the 2010 Europa League for Fulham?
questions.explanation: Clint Dempsey, a chipped finish to complete a comeback from 4-1 down on aggregate. Fulham's greatest night.

questions.question: What stands in the corner of Fulham's ground?
questions.explanation: A cottage, built in 1905 as a pavilion. The players' families watch from its balcony.

questions.question: Fulham's Riverside Stand rebuild, finished in 2024, includes what unusual feature?
questions.explanation: A rooftop swimming pool, among other luxuries. Not every stand has one.

questions.question: Which Fulham striker scored 43 goals in the 2021-22 Championship, a record for the division?
questions.explanation: Aleksandar Mitrović. He broke the record with games to spare and celebrated like every one was a final.

questions.question: Fulham are from which part of London?
questions.explanation: South-west London, in the borough of Hammersmith and Fulham.

questions.question: What is Fulham's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Billy the Badger, who was once sent off by a referee for breakdancing in the corner.

questions.question: What is Hull City's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Tigers, for the amber and black stripes.

questions.question: What is Hull City's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The MKM Stadium, since 2002. It opened as the KC Stadium.

questions.question: What colours are Hull's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Amber and black stripes, like a tiger.

questions.question: In which year was Hull City founded?
questions.explanation: 1904. Rugby league was the game in Hull, and the football club took decades to catch on.

questions.question: In which year did Hull City first reach the top flight of English football?
questions.explanation: 2008, via the play-off final. They had never been in the top division in 104 years.

questions.question: Who scored the winning goal in the 2008 play-off final for Hull?
questions.explanation: Dean Windass, a 39-year-old born in Hull, with a volley from the edge of the box. He cried on the pitch.

questions.question: Which manager took Hull into the Premier League in 2008?
questions.explanation: Phil Brown, remembered for his tan, his headset and one very public team talk.

questions.question: Phil Brown gave a half-time team talk on the pitch in front of the fans at which ground in 2008?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, on Boxing Day, losing 4-0 at the break. It ended 5-1. He later said he regretted it.

questions.question: Hull reached the FA Cup final in 2014 and lost to which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, 3-2 after extra time. Hull had led 2-0 inside eight minutes.

questions.question: Who managed Hull in the 2014 FA Cup final?
questions.explanation: Steve Bruce. Hull got into Europe for the first time as a result, since Arsenal were already in the Champions League.

questions.question: In 2013 Hull's owners tried to rename the club what, and were refused by the FA?
questions.explanation: Hull Tigers. The Allam family argued City was common. The fans and the FA disagreed.

questions.question: What was Hull's home ground before 2002?
questions.explanation: Boothferry Park, which had its own railway station and a supermarket built into one stand.

questions.question: Hull is in which historic county?
questions.explanation: Yorkshire, the East Riding. Hull's full name is Kingston upon Hull.

questions.question: Which club do Hull fans regard as their main rivals?
questions.explanation: Leeds United, across Yorkshire. Grimsby and the Sheffield clubs are the older grudges.

questions.question: Which Portuguese manager led Hull in the Premier League in 2016-17 and later managed Fulham?
questions.explanation: Marco Silva. Hull were relegated, but his reputation survived and Watford and Everton came calling.

questions.question: After relegation from the Premier League in 2017, Hull dropped to League One in which year?
questions.explanation: 2020, finishing bottom of the Championship during the pandemic season.

questions.question: Hull won League One in which year?
questions.explanation: 2021, at the first attempt, bouncing straight back to the Championship.

questions.question: Which Turkish television personality bought Hull City in 2022?
questions.explanation: Acun Ilıcalı, who presents Turkey's version of Survivor. He promised the Premier League.

questions.question: Hull sits on which river?
questions.explanation: The Humber, at the point where the River Hull meets it. Hence the name.

questions.question: What is Hull City's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Roary the Tiger. Not to be confused with the Grimsby one.

questions.question: What is Ipswich Town's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Portman Road, since 1884. The club has never played anywhere else.

questions.question: What is Ipswich Town's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Tractor Boys, which started as a jibe from rival fans about Suffolk farming and got adopted. Also just the Blues.

questions.question: Who are Ipswich Town's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Norwich City. The East Anglian derby, also known as the Old Farm derby, is the biggest game of either club's year.

questions.question: In which year was Ipswich Town founded?
questions.explanation: 1878, though they stayed amateur until 1936 and only joined the Football League in 1938.

questions.question: In which year did Ipswich win the league title?
questions.explanation: 1962, in their very first season in the top division. Nobody has done that since.

questions.question: Who managed Ipswich to the 1962 title and went on to win the World Cup with England?
questions.explanation: Alf Ramsey. He left for England in 1963 and won the World Cup three years later.

questions.question: In which year did Ipswich win the FA Cup?
questions.explanation: 1978, beating Arsenal 1-0 at Wembley. Their only FA Cup.

questions.question: Which European trophy did Ipswich win in 1981?
questions.explanation: The UEFA Cup, over two legs against AZ Alkmaar. Bobby Robson's finest hour at the club.

questions.question: Which manager, later England manager, has a statue outside Portman Road?
questions.explanation: Bobby Robson, Ipswich manager from 1969 to 1982. Alf Ramsey has one too, on the other corner.

questions.question: Which Northern Irish manager took Ipswich from League One to the Premier League in 2023 and 2024?
questions.explanation: Kieran McKenna, back-to-back promotions. Ipswich had been out of the top flight for 22 years.

questions.question: Who did Ipswich beat in the 1981 UEFA Cup final?
questions.explanation: AZ Alkmaar of the Netherlands, 5-4 on aggregate. John Wark scored 14 goals in Europe that season.

questions.question: What colours are Ipswich Town's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Blue shirts with white sleeves, white shorts.

questions.question: Who scored the only goal of the 1978 FA Cup final for Ipswich?
questions.explanation: Roger Osborne, who was so overcome he had to be substituted straight afterwards.

questions.question: Ipswich is in which county?
questions.explanation: Suffolk, on the east coast. Norwich, in Norfolk, is forty miles north.

questions.question: What animal is on the Ipswich Town badge?
questions.explanation: A Suffolk Punch horse, the county's heavy farm breed, standing over a football.

questions.question: Ipswich were founder members of the Premier League in which season?
questions.explanation: 1992-93, having won the second tier the previous year. They were relegated in 1995.

questions.question: In which position did Ipswich finish in 2001, their best Premier League season, under George Burley?
questions.explanation: Fifth, in their first season back up, and into the UEFA Cup. Burley was manager of the year.

questions.question: What tongue-in-cheek name is the Ipswich v Norwich derby sometimes given?
questions.explanation: The Old Farm derby, a joke on Glasgow's Old Firm. The A140 is the road between the two.

questions.question: In which year were Ipswich relegated after just one season back in the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2025, alongside Leicester and Southampton — all three promoted clubs went straight back down.

questions.question: Who is Ipswich Town's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Ray Crawford, 227 goals, most of them in the Ramsey years. He was the first Ipswich player capped by England.

questions.question: What is Leeds United's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Elland Road, since the club was formed in 1919.

questions.question: What colour do Leeds United play in?
questions.explanation: All white, since the 1960s. It was borrowed from Real Madrid.

questions.question: In which year was Leeds United founded?
questions.explanation: 1919, after the previous club, Leeds City, was thrown out of the league for illegal payments.

questions.question: Which manager built the great Leeds team of the 1960s and 70s?
questions.explanation: Don Revie, manager from 1961 to 1974. Two league titles, and a reputation for being hard to beat and hard to like.

questions.question: In which year did Leeds last win the league title?
questions.explanation: 1992, the final season before the Premier League began. Leeds have not finished above United since.

questions.question: Who managed Leeds to the 1992 title, the last English manager to win the top flight?
questions.explanation: Howard Wilkinson, known as Sergeant Wilko. No English manager has won it since.

questions.question: In which year did Leeds reach the semi-finals of the Champions League?
questions.explanation: 2001, losing to Valencia. They had beaten Deportivo and drawn with Barcelona along the way.

questions.question: By which year had Leeds fallen to League One, the third tier, after their financial collapse?
questions.explanation: 2007, three years after leaving the Premier League. They had gambled on Champions League money that stopped.

questions.question: Which Argentine manager took Leeds back to the Premier League in 2020?
questions.explanation: Marcelo Bielsa, who sat on a bucket, ran the players into the ground, and was adored for it.

questions.question: Who are Leeds United's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, in the Roses rivalry: Yorkshire against Lancashire, going back centuries.

questions.question: Which Leeds captain of the Revie era has a statue outside Elland Road?
questions.explanation: Billy Bremner, the fiery Scottish midfielder. Small, red-haired and afraid of nobody.

questions.question: What is Leeds United's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Whites, for the kit. They were also called the Peacocks, after a pub near the ground.

questions.question: Why do Leeds play in all white?
questions.explanation: Don Revie changed the kit in 1961 to copy Real Madrid, the best team in Europe, hoping some of it would rub off.

questions.question: Leeds lost the 1975 European Cup final to which club?
questions.explanation: Bayern Munich, 2-0 in Paris, after two Leeds goals were disallowed. Fans rioted and Leeds were banned from Europe.

questions.question: Leeds returned to the Premier League in 2025 as Championship champions with how many points?
questions.explanation: One hundred, level with Burnley, on the last day. Both clubs went up.

questions.question: What is the name of the Leeds United club song?
questions.explanation: Marching On Together, released as a single in 1972 for the FA Cup final. Sung at every game since.

questions.question: Leeds won the FA Cup in 1972 by beating which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, 1-0 at Wembley, with an Allan Clarke header. Still their only FA Cup.

questions.question: Leeds is in which county?
questions.explanation: West Yorkshire. The white rose on the badge is the county's symbol.

questions.question: Which player did Leeds sell to Manchester United in 1992, a deal they came to regret?
questions.explanation: Eric Cantona, for about £1.2 million. He won four titles in five years at Old Trafford.

questions.question: Which German manager led Leeds to promotion in 2025?
questions.explanation: Daniel Farke, who had already taken Norwich up twice. He knows the Championship.

questions.question: What is Liverpool's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Anfield, since 1892. It had been Everton's ground before a rent row.

questions.question: Which song do Liverpool fans sing before every home match?
questions.explanation: You'll Never Walk Alone, from the musical Carousel, adopted after Gerry and the Pacemakers had a hit with it in 1963.

questions.question: Liverpool's league title in 2025 was the club's how-manyth?
questions.explanation: Twentieth, drawing level with Manchester United's record.

questions.question: How many times have Liverpool won the European Cup or Champions League?
questions.explanation: Six: 1977, 1978, 1981, 1984, 2005 and 2019. More than any other English club.

questions.question: Liverpool came back from 3-0 down to win the 2005 Champions League final against which club?
questions.explanation: AC Milan, in Istanbul. Three goals in six minutes, then penalties. The miracle of Istanbul.

questions.question: Which German managed Liverpool from 2015 to 2024?
questions.explanation: Jürgen Klopp, hugs and heavy metal football. A Champions League and Liverpool's first title in thirty years.

questions.question: In which year did Liverpool end their thirty-year wait for a league title?
questions.explanation: 2020, during the pandemic, with seven games to spare. Fans celebrated outside an empty Anfield.

questions.question: Who is Liverpool's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Ian Rush, 346 goals across two spells in the 1980s and 90s.

questions.question: Which two clubs are Liverpool's main rivals?
questions.explanation: Everton in the Merseyside derby, and Manchester United in the biggest rivalry in English football.

questions.question: The Kop, Anfield's famous stand, is named after what?
options: A hill in the Boer War
questions.explanation: Spion Kop, a hill in South Africa where many Liverpool soldiers died in 1900. The steep terrace reminded people of it.

questions.question: Which Scot managed Liverpool from 1959 to 1974 and has a statue outside Anfield?
questions.explanation: Bill Shankly, who took them up from the second division and built the modern club. The gates are named after him.

questions.question: Which Liverpool manager won three European Cups between 1977 and 1981?
questions.explanation: Bob Paisley, Shankly's quiet assistant, who turned out to be even more successful.

questions.question: Steven Gerrard's long-range equaliser in the 2006 FA Cup final came against which club?
questions.explanation: West Ham, in the last minute, from 35 yards. Liverpool won on penalties. People call it the Gerrard final.

questions.question: Mohamed Salah joined Liverpool in 2017 from which club?
questions.explanation: Roma, for about £37 million. He scored 44 goals in his first season.

questions.question: Virgil van Dijk joined Liverpool in 2018 from which club, for a record fee for a defender?
questions.explanation: Southampton, for £75 million. Liverpool reached two Champions League finals in his first two seasons.

questions.question: Who succeeded Jürgen Klopp as Liverpool manager in 2024 and won the title in his first season?
questions.explanation: Arne Slot, from Feyenoord. Calm where Klopp was loud, and champion within a year.

questions.question: Who did Liverpool beat in the 2019 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Tottenham, 2-0 in Madrid. Salah scored a penalty in the second minute.

questions.question: In the 2019 comeback against Barcelona, who took the quick corner for the winning goal?
questions.explanation: Trent Alexander-Arnold, while Barcelona's defenders were not looking. Divock Origi scored. Corner taken quickly.

questions.question: What bird is on the Liverpool badge?
questions.explanation: The liver bird, the city's symbol, a cormorant with a sprig of seaweed in its beak.

questions.question: Kenny Dalglish joined Liverpool in 1977 from which club?
questions.explanation: Celtic, for £440,000, to replace Kevin Keegan. He became the club's greatest player and then its manager.

questions.question: What is Manchester City's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Etihad Stadium, built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games. Officially the City of Manchester Stadium.

questions.question: Where did Manchester City play before moving to the Etihad in 2003?
questions.explanation: Maine Road, in Moss Side, from 1923. Once the biggest club ground in England.

questions.question: What colour are Manchester City's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Sky blue, since the 1890s. City fans sing Blue Moon.

questions.question: Which Spanish manager took charge of Manchester City in 2016?
questions.explanation: Pep Guardiola, who had won everything at Barcelona and Bayern first. Six league titles in his first eight seasons.

questions.question: In which year was Manchester City bought by Abu Dhabi's Sheikh Mansour?
questions.explanation: 2008, on the last day of the transfer window. Robinho arrived the same day and the modern City began.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City win their first Premier League title?
questions.explanation: 2012, with Agüero's goal in the last seconds of the last game, against QPR, to beat United on goal difference.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City win the treble of league, FA Cup and Champions League?
questions.explanation: 2023, only the second English club to do it after Manchester United in 1999.

questions.question: Who did Manchester City beat in the 2023 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Inter Milan, 1-0 in Istanbul. Rodri scored the goal.

questions.question: How many goals did Erling Haaland score in the 2022-23 Premier League, a record for one season?
questions.explanation: Thirty-six, in his first season in England, beating a record that had stood since 1994.

questions.question: Manchester City became the first club to win how many consecutive English titles in 2024?
questions.explanation: Four in a row, from 2021 to 2024. Nobody had done more than three.

questions.question: Who are Manchester City's rivals in the Manchester derby?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. City spent decades as the noisy neighbours; the noise is louder now.

questions.question: In the 1999 play-off final against Gillingham, who scored City's 95th-minute equaliser?
questions.explanation: Paul Dickov, at Wembley, to force extra time and penalties. City were in the third tier at the time.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City win the European Cup Winners' Cup?
questions.explanation: 1970, beating Górnik Zabrze in Vienna. Their only European trophy before 2023.

questions.question: The Colin Bell Stand at the Etihad is named after a 1960s and 70s midfielder nicknamed what?
questions.explanation: Nijinsky, after the racehorse, because he could run all day.

questions.question: Which Spanish playmaker, nicknamed El Mago, has a statue outside the Etihad?
questions.explanation: David Silva, the magician. Ten seasons, four titles, and a statue next to Agüero's and Kompany's.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City beat Manchester United 6-1 at Old Trafford?
questions.explanation: 2011, on the way to their first title. Balotelli scored and revealed a shirt saying 'Why always me?'

questions.question: What is Manchester City's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Citizens, or the Sky Blues. Fans just say City.

questions.question: The Etihad Stadium is on which side of Manchester?
questions.explanation: East Manchester, in a once-industrial area rebuilt around the stadium and the club's training campus.

questions.question: Which Chilean manager won the Premier League with Manchester City in 2014?
questions.explanation: Manuel Pellegrini, the first manager from outside Europe to win the Premier League.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City win their first league title?
questions.explanation: 1937, and they went down the very next season while scoring more goals than anyone. Typical City, fans said for decades.

questions.question: What is Manchester United's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Old Trafford, since 1910. Bobby Charlton called it the Theatre of Dreams.

questions.question: What is Manchester United's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Red Devils, adopted in the 1960s by Matt Busby, who borrowed it from the Salford rugby team.

questions.question: Manchester United were founded in 1878 under what name?
questions.explanation: Newton Heath LYR, a railway workers' team. They became Manchester United in 1902 when they nearly went bust.

questions.question: Who managed Manchester United from 1986 to 2013?
questions.explanation: Sir Alex Ferguson. Thirteen league titles, two Champions Leagues, and a stand named after him.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester United win the treble of league, FA Cup and Champions League?
questions.explanation: 1999, sealed with two goals in the last three minutes of the Champions League final in Barcelona.

questions.question: Which two substitutes scored the late goals in the 1999 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjær, both off the bench, against Bayern Munich. Football, bloody hell.

questions.question: In which year did the Munich air disaster claim the lives of eight Manchester United players?
questions.explanation: 1958, on the way home from a European Cup game. Matt Busby survived and rebuilt the team.

questions.question: Manchester United became the first English club to win the European Cup in which year?
questions.explanation: 1968, beating Benfica 4-1 at Wembley, ten years after Munich. Bobby Charlton scored twice.

questions.question: Which group of United academy players from the early 1990s is known as the Class of '92?
options: Beckham, Scholes, Giggs and the Nevilles
questions.explanation: David Beckham, Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs, Nicky Butt, Gary and Phil Neville. They won the 1992 FA Youth Cup together.

questions.question: Who is Manchester United's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Wayne Rooney, 253 goals, passing Bobby Charlton's record in 2017.

questions.question: Who are Manchester United's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. Two cities thirty miles apart that have won more than everybody else.

questions.question: Cristiano Ronaldo first joined Manchester United in 2003 from which club?
questions.explanation: Sporting Lisbon, aged eighteen, after tormenting United's players in a friendly. He was given the number seven shirt.

questions.question: How many Premier League titles has Manchester United won?
questions.explanation: Thirteen, all under Ferguson, from 1993 to 2013. Nobody else is close.

questions.question: What was Ole Gunnar Solskjær's nickname as a player?
questions.explanation: The baby-faced assassin, for the innocent looks and the ruthless finishing, often off the bench.

questions.question: Which manager rebuilt United after the war and after Munich, and has a statue at Old Trafford?
questions.explanation: Sir Matt Busby, manager from 1945 to 1969. The road outside the ground is named after him.

questions.question: In which year did Manchester United last win the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2013, Ferguson's final season. He retired as champion and the club has not won it since.

questions.question: What is the name of the stand behind the goal where Manchester United's loudest fans sit?
questions.explanation: The Stretford End, at the west end of Old Trafford.

questions.question: Which American family bought Manchester United in 2005?
questions.explanation: The Glazer family, who own the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Fans have protested against them ever since.

questions.question: Which British billionaire bought a stake in United in 2024 and took over the football side?
questions.explanation: Sir Jim Ratcliffe of INEOS, a boyhood United fan from Failsworth.

questions.question: Manchester United won the 2024 FA Cup by beating which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, 2-1 at Wembley, denying City a second double in a row. Erik ten Hag was still sacked months later.

questions.question: What is Newcastle United's home ground called?
questions.explanation: St James' Park, right in the middle of the city, since 1892.

questions.question: What colours are Newcastle's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Black and white stripes, hence the Magpies. Since 1894.

questions.question: What is Newcastle United's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Magpies, for the stripes. The fans are the Toon Army.

questions.question: Who are Newcastle's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Sunderland, in the Tyne-Wear derby. Twelve miles apart and very little love.

questions.question: Who is Newcastle United's all-time record goalscorer?
questions.explanation: Alan Shearer, 206 goals, a Geordie who turned down Manchester United to come home. He has a statue outside the ground.

questions.question: Newcastle paid a world-record fee for Alan Shearer in 1996. How much?
questions.explanation: £15 million, from Blackburn Rovers. The most anyone had ever paid for a footballer.
